lessons.title: Number sense and estimation
lessons.objective: Use place value, factors, rounding and estimation to judge whether a numerical answer is reasonable.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Estimate before calculating. Compare place values, choose convenient rounded numbers, and use the estimate as a reasonableness check rather than as a replacement for exact calculation. In competition questions, estimation can eliminate impossible options quickly. Always compare the size and units of the estimate with the final answer. Apply the concept to unfamiliar competition conditions, compare at least two possible methods when practical, and verify the final result using an independent check. Pay attention to units, assumptions, boundary cases, and whether the answer actually addresses the question. This turns procedural practice into transferable mathematical reasoning.
examples: Estimate 398 times 21 using 400 times 21. Then compare with the exact result.
Estimate 398 times 21 using 400 times 21. Then compare with the exact result. Extend the same idea to a new context and require the learner to justify the method.
lessons.practical_activity: Estimate the answer first, solve selected questions exactly, and explain any large difference.
lessons.guided_practice: Work through three scaffolded problems for Number sense and estimation: first with full prompts, second with one prompt, and third independently. Require the learner to explain the chosen method before confirming the answer.

lessons.student_task: Create a personal three-step estimation checklist.  Submit a completed response and explain how it demonstrates the lesson objective, including the method, evidence or verification used.
lessons.tutor_guidance: Ask for reasoning, check assumptions and units, and use questions rather than giving the answer. The activity is designed to remain useful for self-learning without a tutor.
lessons.reflection_completion: Record which estimation habit helped you catch an error.  Write one specific strength, one specific error pattern and one concrete action you will take before the next practice attempt.

lessons.title: Fractions, ratios and proportion
lessons.objective: Compare, simplify and apply fractions and ratios in unfamiliar competition problems. Apply the method to unfamiliar competition questions and verify the result.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Fractions describe parts of a whole; ratios compare quantities. Simplify with common factors and compare fractions using benchmarks, common denominators, or cross-multiplication. In proportional situations identify the scale factor before calculating. Keep units and the direction of comparison consistent. Apply the concept to unfamiliar competition conditions, compare at least two possible methods when practical, and verify the final result using an independent check. Pay attention to units, assumptions, boundary cases, and whether the answer actually addresses the question. This turns procedural practice into transferable mathematical reasoning.
examples: Compare 5/8 and 3/5 by cross-multiplication. A recipe uses 2 cups for 5 people; find the amount for 15 people.

lessons.title: Algebraic reasoning
lessons.objective: Translate verbal relationships into equations and solve unknown-value problems with verification. Apply the method to unfamiliar competition questions and verify the result.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Algebra represents unknown quantities using symbols. Identify what is known and unknown, translate the relationship carefully, preserve equality while solving, and substitute the result back into the original statement. Competition questions often hide algebra inside words, tables, or patterns, so the translation step is as important as the calculation. Apply the concept to unfamiliar competition conditions, compare at least two possible methods when practical, and verify the final result using an independent check. Pay attention to units, assumptions, boundary cases, and whether the answer actually addresses the question. This turns procedural practice into transferable mathematical reasoning.

lessons.title: Geometry and measurement
lessons.objective: Apply perimeter, area, angle and unit relationships accurately. Apply the method to unfamiliar competition questions and verify the result.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Perimeter measures boundary length while area measures surface covered. Use straight-line angles totaling 180 degrees and angles around a point totaling 360 degrees. Convert units before combining measurements. For unfamiliar shapes, draw and label the figure and decompose it into familiar parts. Attach correct square units to area and linear units to perimeter. Apply the concept to unfamiliar competition conditions, compare at least two possible methods when practical, and verify the final result using an independent check. Pay attention to units, assumptions, boundary cases, and whether the answer actually addresses the question. This turns procedural practice into transferable mathematical reasoning.
examples: A 12 cm by 7 cm rectangle has perimeter 38 cm and area 84 square cm. Two adjacent angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees.

lessons.title: Patterns and sequences
lessons.objective: Identify sequence rules and justify predicted terms instead of guessing from a short pattern.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Compare consecutive terms. A constant difference suggests an additive rule; a constant multiplier suggests a multiplicative rule. More complex sequences may alternate operations. Test a proposed rule against several terms because matching only two terms is insufficient. State the rule clearly and verify the predicted term. Apply the concept to unfamiliar competition conditions, compare at least two possible methods when practical, and verify the final result using an independent check. Pay attention to units, assumptions, boundary cases, and whether the answer actually addresses the question. This turns procedural practice into transferable mathematical reasoning.
examples: For 4, 7, 10, 13 the difference is 3, so the next terms are 16 and 19. For 3, 6, 12, 24 the multiplier is 2, so the next term is 48.

lessons.title: Data and probability
lessons.objective: Interpret tables and simple data and calculate basic averages and probabilities. Apply the method to unfamiliar competition questions and verify the result.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Read the title, variable, units and scale before calculating. Mean is total divided by count; median is the middle ordered value; mode is the most frequent. For equally likely outcomes, probability is favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes and lies between zero and one. Distinguish evidence from assumptions when interpreting data. Apply the concept to unfamiliar competition conditions, compare at least two possible methods when practical, and verify the final result using an independent check. Pay attention to units, assumptions, boundary cases, and whether the answer actually addresses the question. This turns procedural practice into transferable mathematical reasoning.
examples: For 6,8,8,10,13 the mean is 9, median 8 and mode 8. A bag with 3 red and 7 blue counters has red probability 3/10.

lessons.title: Logical problem solving
lessons.objective: Use constraints, organised cases and elimination to solve unfamiliar logic problems. Apply the method to unfamiliar competition questions and verify the result.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Start by listing what must be true, what cannot be true, and which choices remain. Tables and ordered lists reduce missed cases. Reject a candidate only when a stated condition eliminates it. For multiple conditions, test a final candidate against every condition. If several solutions remain, report that rather than inventing an unstated rule. Apply the concept to unfamiliar competition conditions, compare at least two possible methods when practical, and verify the final result using an independent check. Pay attention to units, assumptions, boundary cases, and whether the answer actually addresses the question. This turns procedural practice into transferable mathematical reasoning.
examples: A three-digit code has a final digit of 5; the first digit is even and the second is greater than the first. Generate candidates systematically.

lessons.title: Multi-step word problems
lessons.objective: Plan multi-stage calculations by identifying the target, intermediate values, operations and units.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Read for meaning before calculating. Identify the final quantity requested and work backwards to determine intermediate values. Do not automatically perform operations in sentence order. Label intermediate results and keep units attached. After solving, estimate the final scale and reread the question to confirm that the requested quantity was actually found. Apply the concept to unfamiliar competition conditions, compare at least two possible methods when practical, and verify the final result using an independent check. Pay attention to units, assumptions, boundary cases, and whether the answer actually addresses the question. This turns procedural practice into transferable mathematical reasoning.
examples: A school buys 8 packs of 24 notebooks and distributes 35. First find 192, then subtract 35 to get 157 notebooks remaining.

lessons.title: Speed, accuracy and verification
lessons.objective: Improve timed performance while using verification methods to catch avoidable errors. Apply the method to unfamiliar competition questions and verify the result.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Competition performance depends on accuracy and decision quality. Separate quick wins, standard problems and high-effort problems. Use estimation, substitution, inverse operations, unit checks or a second method to verify uncertain answers. If a question consumes too much time, mark it and move on rather than sacrificing the whole paper. Return later if time remains. Apply the concept to unfamiliar competition conditions, compare at least two possible methods when practical, and verify the final result using an independent check. Pay attention to units, assumptions, boundary cases, and whether the answer actually addresses the question. This turns procedural practice into transferable mathematical reasoning.
examples: Solve 48 times 25 mentally and verify using a second method. Substitute x=7 into an equation to test whether it is a valid solution.

lessons.title: Integrated mini-mock
lessons.objective: Apply mixed mathematics skills under timed conditions and turn errors into a targeted revision plan.
lessons.core_teaching_content: A mixed assessment requires method selection because the topic is not announced. Classify questions by likely difficulty, manage time deliberately, and analyse errors afterward. Categorise each miss as concept misunderstanding, calculation error, misreading, weak estimation, or time pressure. A score alone is not a diagnosis. Use the error pattern to select the next revision priority and then redo representative questions. Apply the concept to unfamiliar competition conditions, compare at least two possible methods when practical, and verify the final result using an independent check. Pay attention to units, assumptions, boundary cases, and whether the answer actually addresses the question. This turns procedural practice into transferable mathematical reasoning.
examples: A fraction-proportion item tests relationship recognition; a geometry item with the wrong unit tests unit discipline. Explain the reasoning, not just the final answer.

A fraction-proportion item tests relationship recognition; a geometry item with the wrong unit tests unit discipline. Explain the reasoning, not just the final answer. Extend the same idea to a new context and require the learner to justify the method.
